idiom_name: interface value (iface/eface) + any + type assertion / type switch
implementation_notes: An interface value is the pattern built into the runtime: a two-word pair of a type descriptor - an itab for a method interface, the concrete type for the empty interface any - and a data pointer, so a variable of interface type holds any value whose method set satisfies it, including types declared in other packages and never modified. A method interface is the narrow dispatchable form; any is the fully erased form and needs a type assertion or type switch to recover the dynamic type. Satisfaction is structural and implicit (no implements clause), so binding happens by assignment or an explicit conversion. If the set of cases is closed, a generic function (Go 1.18+) or a struct with a discriminator is the simpler, statically checked alternative.
code_sketch:
type Drawer interface{ Draw(w io.Writer) }      // one interface, any satisfier

items := []Drawer{Circle{}, &Square{}}         // unrelated types, no common base
for _, d := range items { d.Draw(os.Stdout) }  // dispatch through the itab

var v any = 42                                 // fully erased; type known at run time
switch x := v.(type) { case int: _ = x; case string: _ = x }
pitfalls: The typed-nil trap: an interface holding a nil *T is non-nil because its type word is set, so err != nil can be true around a nil pointer - return nil explicitly, never a typed nil.

Putting a value (not a pointer) into an interface boxes it: the value is copied to the heap and pointer-receiver methods drop out of its method set, so the type silently fails to satisfy the interface.
any gives up compile-time checking: an unchecked assertion panics at run time, so use the comma-ok form or a type switch and treat the recovered value as untrusted.
